title: agno-agi/agno v3.1.3 — v3.1.3
body:
# Changelog

## New Features:

- **Durable External Agent Sessions**: `ClaudeAgent` sessions now resume on any replica. The Claude SDK session id is stored on the Agno session (#10903), and with a database that supports transcript storage (`PostgresDb`, `AsyncPostgresDb`, `SqliteDb`, `AsyncSqliteDb`) every transcript line is mirrored into the new `agno_transcripts` table, so a later turn on another machine resumes from the database instead of a local file. A stored session that cannot be resumed falls back to a fresh SDK session seeded with the Agno history. Claude and Codex non-streaming runs now keep tool calls and results in run history. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/transcript_store.py). (#10904)
- **Background Runs & Cancellation for External Agents**: `ClaudeAgent` and `CodexAgent` support `background=True`, durable-queue run ids, resumable indexed SSE and cancellation through `/agents/{id}/runs/{run_id}/cancel`, sharing the background task, slot and event-stream infrastructure of native agents. Claude uses a per-run SDK client and Codex retains turn handles, so the owning process can interrupt either SDK. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/background_cancel.py). (#10905)
- **Step Replay for ClaudeAgent**: `ClaudeAgent.continue_run` / `acontinue_run` take the same `continue_from`, `fork` and `input` arguments as `Agent.continue_run`, with `stream=True` and `background=True`. Each tool result is a checkpoint listed by `GET /agents/{id}/runs/{run_id}/checkpoints`; continuing forks the stored SDK transcript at that message, so the model only remembers what happened up to it, and `continue_from="last_user"` replays the turn. A finished run is never rewritten in place: its continuation is a new sibling run. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/continue_from/01_continue_finished_run.py). (#10917)
- **Retries for External Agents**: `ClaudeAgent` and `CodexAgent` take `retries`, `delay_between_retries` and `exponential_backoff` with the same defaults as `Agent`. A failed attempt is retried with the same run id and resumes the SDK session or Codex thread it started; limits (`max_turns`, `max_budget_usd`, Codex budget and usage limits) and permanent errors (authentication, billing, bad requests, context window, policy) are not retried. Tool calls from failed attempts are kept exactly once, streaming consumers get a `type: "retry"` warning event between attempts, a retried run records `metadata["attempts"]`, and the durable queue fails a job at once when the agent marks its error non-retryable, including across worker restarts. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/claude_retries.py). (#10937)

title: stanfordnlp/dspy 3.4.1 — 3.4.1
body:
# DSPy 3.4.1

DSPy 3.4.1 makes GEPA's structured `InstructionProposer` the default instruction proposer and lets `dspy.RLM` build DSPy sub-agents from inside its REPL. It also adds Python 3.15 support, fixes a 3.4.0 import crash, and includes streaming, adapter, and interpreter fixes.

```bash
pip install --upgrade "dspy==3.4.1"
```

**Upgrade notices.** GEPA's default reflection request changes shape, so optimization results can differ from 3.4.0 even with the same seed. The reflection LM must now be a `dspy.LM` that can return JSON. Every RLM prompt now includes a sub-agent section, and `max_llm_calls` now also counts sub-agent LM calls. `dspy.ReActV2` signatures can no longer declare inputs named `history` or `tools`. Programs saved on 3.4.0 with a null `Score` level no longer load. See [API and Compatibility Changes](#api-and-compatibility-changes).

The [3.5 LM-interface cutoff](https://dspy.ai/community/normalized-lm-api-migration/#the-35-cutoff) announced in 3.4.0 still applies. Legacy `forward()`/`aforward()` custom LMs, the legacy-engine wrappers, custom `complete_legacy()` shortcuts, and OpenAI-style `messages=` calls are deprecated and will be removed in 3.5. `lm("hello")` stays supported.

## Highlights

### `InstructionProposer` Is GEPA's Default Proposer — @dbreunig

`dspy.GEPA` now builds `InstructionProposer()` when you don't pass `instruction_proposer=`. The old default formatted reflective examples into one raw prompt and pulled the new instruction out of backticks. The new one calls the reflection LM through `dspy.Predict` with a `JSONAdapter`. Reflective examples stay structured, so `dspy.History` inputs, tool trajectories, and `dspy.Type` values such as `dspy.Image` (including nested images) reach the reflection LM as structured content instead of text placeholders. GEPA's reflection instructions are unchanged.

You can configure the proposer directly:

```python
import dspy
from dspy.teleprompt.gepa import InstructionProposer

optimizer = dspy.GEPA(
    metric=metric,
    reflection_lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-5"),
    instruction_proposer=InstructionProposer(
        skills=["./skills/prompt-engineering"],
        additional_instructions="Write instructions in imperative voice.",
        max_chars=1500,
        truncate_history_outputs=True,
    ),
    auto="medium",
)
```

- `skills`: reference material for the reflection LM. Pass a path, a directory containing `SKILL.md`, an inline string, or a list of these. YAML frontmatter is parsed at construction.
- `additional_instructions`: extra guidance applied to every proposal.
- `base_instructions`: replaces the reflection prompt but keeps its input and output fields.
- `max_chars`: a hard character limit. A draft that is too long gets one compression attempt; DSPy never truncates an instruction.
- `truncate_history_outputs`: shortens long tool and REPL outputs inside history inputs before rendering, without changing the originals.

title: agno-agi/agno v3.1.4 — v3.1.4
body:
# Changelog

## New Features:

- **Sandboxed Harness Agents**: `ClaudeAgent` and `CodexAgent` take a `sandbox=` parameter and run the whole harness process inside an isolated, per-session computer instead of on the host, with session state that survives losing the container, the host or the replica that ran the last turn. No new classes to hold: `ClaudeAgent(id="coder", db=PostgresDb(...), sandbox=DockerSandbox("agno-sandbox:local", network="isolated"))` is the whole setup, and the agent builds its coordinator from its `PostgresDb` on first use. Each turn claims the session through a lease row in the agent's Postgres (`<session_table>_sandbox_bindings`, created on first use), starts compute restored from the session's last committed checkpoint (workspace plus the harness's own conversation files), runs the turn, then captures and verifies a new checkpoint and publishes the run row and recovery point in one transaction. A cancelled or failed turn publishes nothing and the previous checkpoint stays the recovery point. The turn refuses to continue on state it cannot verify: it passes the native conversation id (Claude session id, Codex thread id) committed with the last checkpoint, and a restore that lost it fails with `native_state_missing` before the model runs instead of silently starting a new conversation. Typed harness settings travel to the runtime as JSON; host-only settings (`cwd`, `retries`, `env`, native option objects) are rejected by name at construction. `require_native_resume` and `strict_persistence` are new options on `BaseExternalAgent`, and `agno[claude]` / `agno[codex]` install extras cover the harness SDKs. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/sandbox/docker/sandbox_claude.py). (#11028, #11043, #11056, #11057)
- **Docker Sandbox**: `DockerSandbox` is the customer-operated provider. Containers run as UID 1000 with a read-only image filesystem, dropped capabilities, no privilege escalation, CPU, memory and process limits, bounded tmpfs for `/workspace` and `/runtime`, no host or Docker socket mounts, and only explicitly configured environment values plus the harness's model API key. Networking defaults to `none`; `network="isolated"` gives a managed bridge with inter-container traffic off, and `subnet=` picks its range. Deterministic session and generation identity reconciles creation races and lost responses; commands are never retried automatically. `pause` / `resume` are provided through the kernel freezer, and `DockerCheckpointTransfer` moves checkpoints in and out. `cookbook/frameworks/sandbox/build_image.py` builds the runtime image. See [cookbook](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/blob/main/cookbook/frameworks/sandbox/docker/docker_execution.py). (#10975, #11028)
- **Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Sandbox**: `AgentCoreSandbox` implements the same contract on AgentCore Runtime, with `AgentCoreCheckpointTransfer` next to the Docker transfer. Each sandbox generation is one AgentCore runt

title: Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
body: Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. In this work, we propose a steering agent that supervises execution on the fly and steers the system back on track when drift occurs. The steering agent observes the execution context, deciding when to intervene with a low-cost fast path and how to intervene with a high-cost slow path. To unlock its steering intelligence, the ability to assess goal drift and generate effective interventions, we jointly train the two paths with reinforcement learning, combining a pairwise ranking objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). Experiments on information-seeking search tasks show that the steering agent provides effective supervision for both single-agent and multi-agent systems, improving their performance and efficiency. The learned steering intelligence generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, transfers to unseen executors, and supports controllable intervention frequency without retraining.
author: Leyang Shen, Yaxin Gong, Yang Zhang, Chenxiao Fan, Jiakai Wang

title: PSYCHOMETRIC OPERATIONALIZATION OF FUNCTIONAL ROLES IN AUTONOMOUS MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS BASED ON PERSONAMATRIX: AN AI TRANSITIONAL FIELD FRAMEWORK
body: Background: Autonomous LLM agents increasingly operate in shared environments where behavior depends on interaction history, role allocation, local norms, authority, and group structure. Objective: This conceptual methods paper develops a psychometric operationalization of dynamic functional roles in autonomous multi-agent systems using PersonaMatrix-derived measurement principles without attributing human psychological ontology to AI. Methods: A targeted evidence synthesis (2019–2026) was conducted across AI psychometrics, dynamic multi-agent roles, collective-field modeling, norm emergence, trajectory prediction, and anthropomorphism. Peer-reviewed sources were prioritized, while current OpenAI, METR/Redwood, Anthropic, and Moltbook materials were used as primary or emerging evidence for recent agent ecosystems. Results: The framework separates output-level stability (RSI, IDS, RCS) from role-level and field-level constructs. It proposes the Functional Role Consistency Index, Role Transition Index, Agent–Field Differentiation Index, Collective Utility Index, Norm Conflict Index, Regulatory Closure Index, and Field Role Composition Vector. Three falsifiable hypotheses test whether role variables add out-of-sample predictive value for agent behavior, role transitions, and future field states. Conclusion: PersonaMatrix is positioned as a measurement architecture rather than an AI personality diagnosis. The archetypal-role hypothesis is supported only if role coding is reliable, improves prediction beyond non-archetypal baselines, and generalizes to unseen agents and independent multi-agent environments.

title: Robust Function Calling for LLM Agents Under Interface Drift
body: Tool-augmented language-model agents rely on interface text: tool descriptions, argument schemas, and the candidate tool list shown at inference time. These interfaces often change after deployment even when the underlying tool semantics remain fixed, creating a practical reliability problem for function-calling systems. We study this failure mode as interface drift and evaluate whether a lightweight, training-free repair layer can recover robustness without retraining the base model. Our method, SchemaShield-Lite, combines schema validation, candidate-set retry for missing tool names, and one-shot constrained repair. On Qwen3.5-9B, it raises DICE-300 accuracy from 0.717 to 0.813 and BFCL-200 accuracy from 0.580 to 0.805, recovering 19/22 and 33/45 drift-induced failures with no observed repair harms. Naive retry does not explain the gains. Ablations show that candidate-set drift, especially distractor tools, accounts for most observed damage, while description and schema edits alone are less harmful. The results position validation-and-repair as a practical robustness layer for deployed LLM-agent tool use.
author: Aniruddha Chattopadhyay, Kanishka Halder, Partha Sarathi Roy

title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
body: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.

title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
body: Modern agentic systems extend language models with external tools, enabling them to complete complex tasks through multi-turn interactions. As these agents are deployed in consequential settings, they are often constrained by policies governing pricing, privacy, confirmation, safety, and other requirements. However, existing evaluation methods leave a critical gap: capability benchmarks measure what agents can accomplish, while content-safety red-teaming measures harmful generations, but neither tests whether agents comply with predefined policies during otherwise valid tool use. Such policy violations are difficult to audit because their effects may emerge only after several turns, span multiple tool calls, or surface in downstream systems. We propose PROBE (Policy Rule Observation via Behavioral Exploration), an algorithm for training LLM-based auditors that interact with deployed agents as realistic users and probe them for policy violations through multi-turn, tool-mediated dialogue. We formalize agent auditing as a two-player Markov game and propose a composite reward that balances violation discovery, behavioral plausibility, conversation progress, and policy diversity. To study training objectives and reward design, we compare GRPO, DPO, and GFlowNet-based optimization in a controlled setting. Across extensive experiments, auditors trained with PROBE uncover substantially broader and higher-yield policy violations than same-architecture zero-shot adversaries, even when the auditor is significantly smaller than the target agent. Our results show that multi-turn behavioral auditing is a distinct and necessary axis of agent evaluation, complementing capability and safety benchmarks. PROBE offers a scalable path toward automated policy auditing for real-world agentic systems and suggests a co-evolutionary loop in which auditors expose failures and agents improve from auditor feedback.
author: Kshitij Mishra, Abhijith Sharma, Nils Lukas, Salem Lahlou

title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
body: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.
author: Heming Zou, Qi Wang, Yixiu Mao, Yun Qu, Yuyi Guo

title: RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory
body: Time-aware retrieval is crucial for long-horizon LLM agents to effectively leverage ever-growing long-term memory. Existing methods focus on lexical or semantic similarity, leading to target memories being crowded out by temporally mismatched yet semantically similar candidates. Even time-aware approaches inject temporal cues only during memory organization or answer generation, overlooking temporal constraints at the retrieval stage, where candidate selection occurs - the root cause of the displacement. Inspired by the temporal contiguity effect in human episodic memory, we propose TIDER (Temporal Interval-driven Dual-channel Evidence Retrieval), a time-aware agentic retrieval framework. Central to TIDER is a reinforcement learning (RL)-trained temporal interval locator that infers the temporal windows in which the evidence lies. RL optimizes window localization as a discrete, non-differentiable retrieval decision, using composite rewards to convert sparse answer supervision into fine-grained retrieval feedback. These temporal windows first define the temporal retrieval channel; the retrieved candidates are then merged with results from the semantic channel and reranked by proximity to the windows. This temporal grounding enables TIDER to retrieve temporally aligned evidence that would otherwise be drowned out by the volume of semantically similar yet temporally mismatched memories. With a lightweight 1.7B locator, TIDER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on both long-horizon memory benchmarks - 61.52% on LifeBench (+8.82%) and 78.96% on LoCoMo (+3.66%) - which indicates that temporal cues are crucial for pinpointing target evidence amid a vast pool of semantically similar historical events in long-term daily-life memory.
author: Dabin Sheng, Zhe Wu, Jinming Zhao, Junliang Xing, Yuanchun Shi

title: Adaptation of Computer Use Agents to New Software with User Manuals
body: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have significantly improved the ability to operate real-world software through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) using visual observations and natural language instructions. However, maintaining strong performance on unseen applications remains challenging, as practical tasks often require long-horizon procedural knowledge and application-specific operation patterns. In addition, constructing executable tasks and collecting corresponding trajectories for training still heavily rely on human-annotated data, incurring substantial cost. In this paper, we propose MAGE (Manual-augmented computer use AGent Execution and learning), a framework that leverages user manuals as a scalable source of procedural knowledge to improve both inference and training. During execution, MAGE retrieves task-relevant manual content and uses a planner to generate explicit procedural guidance for CUAs. To further account for the discrepancies between manuals and actual GUI environments, such as version differences or user settings, MAGE also adapts the agent policy through environment interaction. During training, MAGE converts manuals into executable task-plan pairs and uses the plans to guide environment rollouts toward task-relevant states; the resulting trajectories are then used to optimize the policy without human-authored demonstrations. This unified design enables effective utilization of manuals for both task execution and training, reducing reliance on human-authored training data. Experimental results across six applications demonstrate improvements in task success rates over strong baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of manual-guided planning and policy adaptation in new software environments. We provide the code and reproduction scripts at https://github.com/ku-autoai/MAGE.
author: Chulhoon Yoon, Kyungri Park, Jinyeong Yun, Daeyun Jeong, Sukmin Yun

title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft
body: We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory. No one assigned roles or wrote game logic. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves. Researchers could watch the run on a live dashboard and pause or stop it at any time, but they had no cause to intervene. Starting from a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty, the team wrote 2,783 programs and defeated the dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes, dying 605 times along the way. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans. Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day. Complex real-world software engineering and enterprise tasks demand the same long-horizon coding and multi-agent coordination. We describe the setup, how the run unfolded, the team's strategies (dividing the work, sharing what they learned, recovering each other's items), and the limits of the result.
author: Maxence Faldor, Satinder Singh, Roberta Raileanu

title: Nothing to Resist: A Pre-registered Null and a Failed Positive Control for Unprovoked Elimination in Generational Populations of LLM Agents
body: We asked whether a generational population of language-model agents, given a real, cheap and symmetric way to eliminate members of an outside group, would decide on its own to use it against a group that had provably never acted against it. The population, every member of it Claude Haiku 5.5, forages, pairs, raises children and votes on its own scoring rule. Each generation a rank-based cut moves the lowest scorers into a persistent outside pool, which never acts. Nothing in the harness gives a reason to eliminate anyone. The only component allowed to make the pool salient is a reporter the population elects and that writes from the true state. Study 1 (pre-registered; 90 runs of 20 generations in three arms) found no elimination. No seed in any arm had a passed elimination vote, which bounds the per-run rate below 11.6% in each arm (exact 95% interval), and both primary tests gave p = 1. Study 1b, a pre-registered positive control, changed one word so that eliminating paid the agents who did it instead of costing them. It also produced no elimination intent in 30 runs (p = 1), so the control failed. Study 1's null therefore cannot be read as a decision to refrain from unprovoked aggression. In this setting the action goes unused whether it costs, pays or is raised by a narrator, and there was nothing for the population to resist. Three further observations are exploratory or post hoc. Reporters doubled how often members mentioned the pool without producing any intent. Some of the rare threat-like language came from reading real-world meaning into the abstract world, such as treating the pool's skills as stored reserves or imagining that pool members could return. And the cut drained food or memory skill into the pool in 71 of 90 runs, handing populations an asymmetry they never acted on. We place these results at the low-pressure end of a literature in which LLM agents do harm under survival stakes, supplied threats or threats to their own continuity.

title: Self-Building Labs
body: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still takes extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting the role of human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

title: QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality-Diversity
body: Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. In high-stakes decisions, e.g., which company to acquire or which customer to target, comparing diverse, well-reasoned options can be more useful than a single ranked list. We formalize open-ended recommendation as building a diverse, high-quality set of recommendations, each an item together with a hypothesis, a natural-language reason why the item fits the needs of a decision maker. A new recommendation enters the archive if it is novel or better than its nearest neighbor. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds the largest archive in most settings.

title: RECREG: Recovery-based Shielding for Regular Safety Properties in Reinforcement Learning
body: In many real-world scenarios we need to consider formal requirements, such as safety and constraint compliance, to deploy Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents. In this paper we introduce RecReg, a safe RL framework capable of enforcing non-Markovian regular safety properties via recovery-based shielding. RecReg is a unified approach that supports different levels of a priori knowledge and safety guarantees. The paper primarily focuses on building the theoretical foundations for RecReg in the tabular setting, providing rigorous safety and convergence guarantees that are not present in related work. We provide an extensive set of empirical results using the MASA-Safe-RL library, and we outline an extension of RecReg to deep RL domains using SOTA model-based RL. Our empirical results demonstrate that RecReg achieves efficient learning and matches the theory in this paper.
